421.quote_or_event: “The True Guru has placed the sword of spiritual wisdom in my hands; I have overcome and slain the Messenger of Death.”
421.explanation: In Raag Vadhans Guru Ram Das describes spiritual wisdom (gian) as a sword given by the Guru, with which the seeker defeats the forces of death.
421.tie_back: The Kural calls wisdom a weapon against ruin and a fortress enemies cannot breach; Guru Ram Das likewise calls wisdom a weapon that defeats the gravest enemy.
421.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 574, Raag Vadhans, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
421._accuracy_note: A strong fit on wisdom as a weapon; Gurbani's enemy is spiritual death and the vices rather than worldly ruin, and the fortress image is absent.

422.quote_or_event: “Taking up the sword of spiritual wisdom, she struggles with her mind, and hope and desire are smoothed over in her mind.”
422.explanation: In Raag Maaroo Guru Nanak describes the soul-bride using spiritual wisdom to fight her own mind until its restless desires are stilled.
422.tie_back: The Kural defines wisdom as not letting the mind run where it likes, holding it from evil and steering it to good; Guru Nanak shows wisdom wrestling the mind and stilling its cravings.
422.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1022, Raag Maaroo (Solhe), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
422._accuracy_note: A strong fit on wisdom restraining the wandering mind; the Kural also stresses steering the mind toward the good, which this line leaves implicit.

423.quote_or_event: “From the True Guru, I have obtained a discriminating intellect; the Guru has revealed the spiritual wisdom of God.”
423.explanation: In Raag Todee Guru Ram Das calls the discriminating intellect (bibek budh), the power to tell true from false and good from bad, a gift of the Guru.
423.tie_back: The Kural defines wisdom as seeing the truth of whatever is said, whoever says it; Guru Ram Das prizes the same discernment as bibek budh.
423.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 711, Raag Todee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
423._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both value the power to discern truth, but Gurbani presents it as the Guru's gift and does not address weighing claims regardless of who speaks.

424.quote_or_event: “Those words are acceptable, which, when spoken, bring honor.”
424.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak says that only speech that earns honour, before people and before God, is true speech.
424.tie_back: The Kural defines wisdom as speaking so that the meaning lands easily in the listener, and grasping subtle meaning in others; Guru Nanak likewise sets a standard for speech worth speaking.
424.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
424._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both judge speech, but Guru Nanak's standard is honour and truth, not clarity, and the Kural's second half on subtle listening is missing.

425.quote_or_event: “They alone are my friends, who travel along with me; and in that place, where the accounts are called for, they appear standing with me.”
425.explanation: In Raag Soohee Guru Nanak says true friends are those who stay with a person to the very end, even at the final reckoning.
425.tie_back: The Kural praises befriending the worthy and keeping that friendship steady, without blooming and then closing; Guru Nanak names steadfastness to the end as the test of true friendship.
425.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
425._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on steady friendship; Guru Nanak speaks of the companions who stand by the soul at the divine reckoning, read by some commentators as one's good deeds.

426.quote_or_event: “In the midst of this world, do seva, and you shall be given a place of honor in the Court of the Lord.”
426.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak teaches that the spiritual life is lived in the world through service, not by leaving it.
426.tie_back: The Kural defines wisdom as living in harmony with the world as the worthy do; Guru Nanak likewise places the right life within the world, through seva.
426.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
426._accuracy_note: Partial: both endorse engaged life in the world, but the Kural speaks of conforming to the worthy, while Guru Nanak speaks of service and honour before God.

427.quote_or_event: “If someone focuses on the Lord beforehand, then why should he be punished?”
427.explanation: In one of the Babarvani hymns on Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak says that people who are mindful beforehand would not suffer such punishment; Sahib Singh reads it as keeping one's duty in mind in good time.
427.tie_back: The Kural says the wise know beforehand what is coming; Guru Nanak says that being mindful in good time spares one the suffering that comes later.
427.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
427._accuracy_note: A strong fit on timely foresight; in Gurbani it is mindfulness of God and duty rather than worldly prediction of consequences.

428.quote_or_event: “Without the Fear of God, no one crosses over the world-ocean. This Fear of God adorns the Love of the Lord.”
428.explanation: In Raag Gauree Guru Nanak teaches that reverent fear of God (bhau) is necessary and that it adorns rather than opposes love.
428.tie_back: The Kural calls it folly not to fear what should be feared and wisdom to fear it; Guru Nanak names the one fear that must never be lost, the fear of God.
428.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 151, Raag Gauree Gwaarayree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
428._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both treat rightly placed fear as wisdom, but the Kural means prudent fear of harmful acts, while Gurbani's bhau is reverent awe of God that frees one from other fears.

429.quote_or_event: “The hot wind does not even touch one who is under the Protection of the Supreme Lord God.”
429.explanation: In Raag Bilaaval Guru Arjan says that one who takes refuge in God is not even touched by the scorching wind of affliction.
429.tie_back: The Kural says no calamity can make the wise tremble, because they guard against it in advance; Guru Arjan says affliction cannot even touch one sheltered in God.
429.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 819, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
429._accuracy_note: Partial: the result (calamity cannot touch one) matches, but the protection comes from God's refuge, not from the person's own foresight.

430.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, those who do not think of the Guru, and who think of themselves as clever, shall be left abandoned in the field, like the scattered sesame.”
430.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak says the self-satisfied who ignore the Guru are like hollow sesame plants left behind in an empty field.
430.tie_back: The Kural says those without wisdom have nothing, whatever else they own; Guru Nanak says those without the Guru's wisdom, however clever they think themselves, are left empty and abandoned.
430.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
430._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit for the Kural's negative half; the positive claim that the wise possess everything is not stated, and the wisdom meant is the Guru's.
